newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl seeks reflected glory at Erhard ceremony.
newsitem.headline: Kohl seeks reflected glory at Erhard ceremony.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl took time off from Bonn's tax and pension feuds on Wednesday to reach for reflected glory at a ceremony in honour of Ludwig Erhard, the father of Germany's post-war "economic miracle."

Marking the 100th anniversary of Erhard's birth, Kohl was host to about 2,000 guests for an official commemoration paying tribute to Erhard who launched the deutschemark, freed the economy from over-regulation and saw growth and exports boom.

Kohl portrayed the late politician as a visionary whose "social market economy" was still relevant for Germany. But he avoided specific lessons for his own government now mired in fierce struggles over cutting the cosy welfare state it produced.

"Without him, the economic prosperity and social peace that has effectively lasted down to this day would not have been conceivable," Kohl said in opening remarks to an audience including Luxembourg's Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker.
"We all see his work is relevant for us today. We Germans have a lot to thank him for."

The cigar-chomping Erhard, who died in 1977, was Bonn's first economics minister from 1949 to 1963 and then its second chancellor from 1963 to 1966. His 100th birthday will fall on February 4 but the ceremony was scheduled for Wednesday.

Kohl later scrapped a planned speech after a former associate of Erhard made a stirring appeal for deregulation of Germany's rule-bound economy and urged politicians to make sound long-term policies rather than simply popular headlines.

"Be wary of a socially strangulated economy," warned Fritz Hellwig, a retired politician from the ranks of Kohl's and Erhard's Christian Democratic Union (CDU). Officials said Kohl dropped his speech because the ceremony was running late.

The emphasis Kohl and Hellwig put on making the economy more competitive prompted howls from the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), who said the centre-right government was forgetting the social part of Erhard's message.
"This coalition has betrayed its social conscience," SPD party manager Franz Muentefering said. "It is not fighting unemployment. It has proposed an unfair tax system."

Erhard's "social market economy," with its stress on consensus between management and labour and its strong safety net to soften the market's blows, helped underpin West Germany's democratic rebirth from the ashes of the Third Reich.
He became a legend by introducing the deutschemark in 1948, liberalising a shattered economy and presiding over the "economic miracle" of the 1950s.
When his centre-right coalition collapsed in 1966, the supposed "stagnation" besetting Bonn was an unusually slow growth rate of "only" 2.5 percent.
But this once-lean welfare state, which made West Germany relatively immune to the aggressive free market policies pursued in Britain and the United States in the 1980s, has grown fat over the years.
Although Kohl preaches the virtures of Erhard's policies, he has had less success in unshackling the economy and weaning Germans off the comforts of the welfare state.

He has stood aside in recent weeks to have his cabinet ministers fight for controversial tax reforms and cuts in the pension system, both meant in part to keep Bonn's deficit down in preparation for Europe's single currency.
Kohl's bid to link his unpopular economic policies with the glow of Erhard's legacy was clearly on view at the ceremony.

A short film on Erhard's life ended with a shot of a young-looking Kohl standing in the background in 1977 as the master said of the 1950s boom: "It was no miracle. It was all thought up and thought out -- and not by me alone."
